opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing FAIR needed, and what made it work in the early days, was a real separation between long-term research and product pressure. When we created FAIR in 2013, the deal with Mark was very clear: we would do open research, publish everything, release code, and work on problems that might take five or ten years to pay off. That's what attracted top scientists. People don't come to an industry lab to optimize click-through rates. They come because they can work on the big questions and still have a voice in the scientific community.

What happens in any large company, and this isn't unique to Meta, is that when a technology suddenly becomes commercially hot, as LLMs did after ChatGPT, there's enormous pressure to pull everyone toward the short term. Product groups want results next quarter. That's legitimate. But if you let that pressure absorb your research organization entirely, you lose the next generation of ideas. And I've been saying for a while that LLMs are not the path to human-level intelligence. They're useful, but they don't understand the physical world, they don't have persistent memory, they can't really reason or plan. So you need a group working on what comes after: world models, joint embedding architectures like JEPA, systems that learn from video and observation the way babies and animals do.

So organizationally, I'd say three things. First, protect a research group with a long horizon and keep it insulated from product roadmaps. Second, stay committed to openness. Open research and open-source models aren't charity. They make the whole ecosystem progress faster, and the company benefits from that. Third, have a good interface between research and product, so ideas that mature can get picked up by people whose job is to build products, without forcing researchers to become product engineers.

The tension between those things never fully goes away. You have to manage it deliberately. And if you don't, the best researchers will go somewhere they can do the work they believe in. Sometimes that means starting something new themselves.

r001.rationale: The response calls for a protected research group and a good interface so mature research can move into product development.

r002.rationale: It describes short-term pressure generally, but does not say that this pressure caused Meta GenAI to stop interacting with FAIR.

r003.rationale: It discusses short-term pressure and LLM limitations, but does not say that the pressure made Meta GenAI conservative in LLM development.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you have to understand how FAIR was set up in the first place. When I joined at the end of 2013, Mark and Mike Schroepfer basically gave me a mandate to build a research lab that would operate on the open research model: publish everything, release the code, hire the best people and let them work on long-horizon problems without asking them to justify every quarter. That's the model that produced PyTorch, Detectron, the self-supervised learning work, the large language model work, the whole lineage. And it worked because the lab was insulated from the product organization. Research was not supposed to be a service bureau for product teams.

Now, what does the organization need to carry that forward? I'd say three things.

First, you need a layer in between. Pure research is not enough. You need a group whose job is to take ideas out of the lab, scale them up, make them robust, and hand them to the product side. At Meta that took a while to get right. For years, things would come out of FAIR and either get picked up heroically by some product team or they would just sit there. The creation of things like the Applied Machine Learning group, and then later the GenAI organization, was an attempt to build that bridge. Whether it's structured well is a different question, but the structural need is real.

Second, you need leadership at the very top that understands that research has a long time constant. The things we were working on in 2015 and 2016, like self-supervised learning, became important seven or eight years later. If you measure a research lab on a two-year horizon, you will kill it. That's what happened to a lot of industrial labs historically, Bell Labs being the obvious example. Meta has been relatively good at this because Mark has a long attention span, but it requires constant defense. There is always pressure to turn research into engineering.

And third, which is the one I'm most insistent about, you need to maintain the openness. The moment you decide that your research is a trade secret, you stop being able to recruit the best people, you stop getting the feedback and the contributions from the outside, and you lose the ecosystem effect. The reason PyTorch and Llama had the impact they had is precisely because they were open. So organizationally, the commitment to openness has to come from the top and it has to be protected from the people who, in a moment of competitive panic, want to close everything.

The thing I would add is that the generative AI frenzy has made this harder, not easier. There's enormous pressure to put all the resources on scaling LLMs because that's what the competition is doing. But my view, and I've been saying this for a long time, is that LLMs are not the path to human-level intelligence. So the organization also needs to tolerate people like me saying, no, we're going to work on world models and planning and joint-embedding architectures, even if that doesn't ship a product next quarter. If the structure can't tolerate that kind of disagreement, then it can't carry research forward. It can only carry engineering forward, and that's a different thing.

r001.rationale: The response says Meta needed a group between research and product to scale up ideas and hand them to product teams, citing Applied Machine Learning and GenAI as attempts to build that bridge.

r002.rationale: It describes pressure to prioritize LLM scaling and says GenAI was an attempt to bridge research and product, but does not attribute GenAI’s lack of interaction with FAIR to short-term pressure.

r003.rationale: It says competitive pressure pushed resources toward scaling LLMs, but does not say that this made Meta GenAI conservative in LLM development.

astra-6.text: I think what was needed was an organization that could bridge long-term research and product development. FAIR’s role is to explore ideas whose usefulness may not be obvious yet. You want to preserve that freedom. But you also need teams that can take a promising research result, do the engineering, scale it up, and turn it into something people can use. Those are different activities, with different time horizons. The challenge is to connect them without making every research project depend on an immediate product application.

r001.rationale: It says Meta needed an organization to connect long-term FAIR research with engineering, scaling, and product development.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute a lack of interaction between Meta GenAI and FAIR to short-term pressure.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss short-term pressure making Meta GenAI conservative in LLM development.

sol-6.1.text: I think the key was to build an organization that could take research ideas and turn them into systems at scale. FAIR was designed for open-ended research, where you pursue ideas that might take years to work. You need to preserve that freedom. But you also need teams with the engineering resources, computing infrastructure, and product connections to develop the ideas that become promising. Those are different activities, with different timelines. The challenge is to connect them so that research can have an impact without making immediate product requirements the agenda for all research.

r001.rationale: It describes connecting open-ended FAIR research with engineering resources and product teams to develop promising ideas into systems at scale.

r002.rationale: It does not say Meta GenAI failed to interact with FAIR or attribute such a lack of interaction to short-term pressure.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss Meta GenAI’s approach to LLM development or say short-term pressure made it more conservative.
